It is often suggested by futurists and economists that we have experienced several phases of industrial revolution across the Industrial Age. The first was the introduction of centralized mass production and the core paradigms that supported it, in particular large scale corporate capitalism. This era was characterized by the reliance on machine tool production. energy from coal and water, the early steam engine, and steam powered transportation.

The next revolution was the introduction of general electrification and industrial automation. Mechanically powered machine tool systems facilitating and amplifying still largely human production gave way to progressively more sophisticated, intricate, yet highly specialized electromechanical systems that could replace human labor outright. This era was characterized by the increasing reliance on oil and gas energy in addition to coal and the distribution of energy as electric power. Steam engines were supplanted by the internal combustion engine, the turbine, and the electric motor. This era is also characterized by the transformation of the urban habitat to a focus largely on commerce and corporate management with the ejection of industry and the middle-class to the suburbs.

The next revolution was the digital revolution--also called the Information Age--with the introduction of digital computers and large scale information systems. This era brought us the beginning of the de-centralization of production with concepts of production/distribution networking. Ideas like 'just-in-time' production scheduling, the heavy reliance on standardized interchangeable modular components, etc. It was anticipated that this revolution would also usher in the era of Total Automation, but artificial intelligence proved a bit farther off. However, information technology did begin the erosion of the core paradigms of the Industrial Age and the de-industrialization of the original western industrial nations; the off-loading of production to the developing world through Globalization as the 'superpowers' sought to become--as I like to put it--the Pointy-Haired Bosses of the world.

It is now said that we are today entering the fourth industrial revolution, the era of 'smart' automation, also referred to as the emerging Post-Industrial Age as it is characterized by the general trend of 'demassification' in production, economics, culture, and political power. Also, demassification of energy hegemonies with the advance of renewable energy technology. This is what Alvin Toffler referred to as the Third Wave. The original paradigms of the Industrial Age have been eroded from within by the technologies on which it became dependent, the concept of centralized mass production supplanted by dispersed, networked, increasingly local, increasingly on-demand production afforded by new smart automation affording greater production flexibility at progressively smaller scales.

The factory as we have known it is dead. In the year 2000 the number of consumer goods produced in so-called 'job shops' (small contract production shops mostly in Asia) surpassed that of traditional factories and never went back. Production became a generalized commodity, akin to the processing power of a computer, and corporations began to divest of ownership of production as the capital overhead--the cost of money--became a drag on competitiveness.

With the obsolescence of centralized mass production comes the erosion of capitalism as it was premised across the Industrial Age on the necessity of creating gigantic pools of capital and putting it in the hands of a certain elite for the purposes of initiating mass production needing gigantic facilities and machinery and huge minimum production volumes. Now the systems of production are not only getting smarter, they are getting more flexible, shrinking in physical size and cost, and shrinking in minimum volumes of production toward manufacture-on-demand. They are becoming self-replicating. They are on a long-term trend of disappearing into the infrastructure. One can now initiate more kinds of production out of pocket than ever before--if you even need to own it at all--and the number of things you can't competitively manufacture in the space of a 2-4 car garage is slowly but steadily shrinking. Production is slowly merging with automated distribution. Amazon is destined to evolve into a combined production/distribution web that eventually becomes a generic municipal utility, like water, power, and the internet. No AI or nanotechnology are needed for this evolutionary trend, but they will greatly accelerate it as it emerges.

We commonly worry about the fate of jobs and workers in an impending era of total automation, but capital is in the same boat, along with many institutions whose existence were integral to Industrial Age paradigms that no longer make sense. The very concept of the nation-state as we know it is due for disruption. And this is why we now debate concepts like Universal Basic Income. Businesses can no longer keep telling workers to adapt or die. Bankers can no longer keep telling each other smile or die.
